examples: The board finally acceded to the union's demand for a wage review.
She acceded to his request that the letter be read aloud.
The city acceded to publishing the inspection reports online.
After three days of talks, the company acceded.
The government has never acceded to a single one of those conditions.
He acceded to the plan only because refusing would have cost him the contract.
entries.русский: уступить, пойти навстречу — офиц./юр.: согласиться на требование (accede to + сущ./-ing)
entries.patterns: accede + to + noun phrase · accede + to + -ing · accede (intransitive)
entries.never: accede to do something and accede that — accede is never followed by an infinitive or a that-clause, and it never takes a direct object. The to is a preposition, so what follows is a noun or an -ing form: acceded to the request, acceded to releasing the records.
entries.watch out: the same verb also means take office (acceded to the throne) and join a treaty (acceded to the convention). All three senses share the to.
entries.reports: formal agreement to a demand or request made by someone with a claim on you — where agree is neutral and consent grants permission, accede concedes ground.

examples: She accepted the offer without asking about the salary.
I accept that the numbers don't support my original estimate.
The committee accepted his resignation the same afternoon.
He never accepted the verdict as fair.
They accepted our apology and the matter ended there.
Nobody at the table accepted that the delay was anyone's fault.
entries.русский: принять, согласиться — принять предложенное; либо признать что-то верным (accept that)
entries.patterns: accept + noun phrase · accept + that-clause · accept + noun phrase + as + noun phrase · accept + -ing? (see below)
entries.never: accept to do something — one of the most persistent errors made by speakers of French, Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese, whose equivalents all take the infinitive. English accept has no infinitive frame at all. Repairs: He agreed to help, He accepted the job, He accepted an invitation to speak. Nor accept someone to do something: ✗ They accepted him to join the board → They accepted him as a board member, or They agreed to let him join the board.
entries.the -ing question: accept takes a gerund only when the gerund is a genuine noun phrase naming a thing accepted — She accepted losing the deposit (she came to terms with it). It cannot mean agreed to do it: ✗ He accepted driving us to the airport is wrong for He offered to drive us.
entries.two speech acts: accept an offer is agreement; accept that something is true is concession. Only the second takes a that-clause: I accept that I was wrong.
entries.reports: taking what is offered, or conceding a point — unlike agree, it presupposes something already on the table to be taken or granted.
entries.see also: agree, consent, decline, refuse, reject, turn down

examples: The minority shareholders acquiesced rather than fund another lawsuit.
She acquiesced in the reorganization but made her objections part of the record.
Congress acquiesced to the transfer of funds for two full budget cycles.
By saying nothing for six months, the landlord had acquiesced in the sublet.
He acquiesced to being interviewed only after his attorney approved the questions.
Nobody acquiesces to a rule they were never told about.
entries.русский: молча согласиться, смириться — книжн.: не возражать, не одобряя по существу
entries.type: reporting verb — reluctant or silent agreement
entries.patterns: acquiesce (intransitive) · acquiesce + in + noun phrase / -ing · acquiesce + to + noun phrase / -ing
entries.never: acquiesce to do something and acquiesce that — no infinitive, no that-clause, and no direct object. Repairs: acquiesced in the decision, acquiesced to the new terms, acquiesced in being reassigned.
entries.in vs. to: traditional and legal usage prefers acquiesce in; acquiesce to is now at least as common in American writing and is not an error. In is the safer choice in formal prose.
entries.reports: agreement given by not objecting — it reports compliance without endorsement, which no other verb in this group carries.

examples: He agreed to look at the engine before the weekend.
Everyone at the meeting agreed that the deadline was unrealistic.
She agreed to the terms but asked for the payment schedule in writing.
I don't agree with him about much, but he was right about the roof.
We finally agreed on a date in early October.
They couldn't agree where to hold the reception.
It was agreed that the vote would be taken by secret ballot.
entries.русский: согласиться — принять предложение или мнение; нейтральный глагол всей группы
entries.type: reporting verb — agreement, acceptance of a proposal
entries.patterns: agree + to-infinitive · agree + that-clause · agree + to + noun phrase · agree + with + person / statement · agree + on/about + noun phrase / -ing · agree + wh-clause · agree + noun phrase (a price, a date, a text) — British English only · passive: it was agreed that…
entries.never: agree someone to do something — agree never takes a personal object before its complement. Repairs: agreed to let her go, agreed that she could go, agreed with her. Also agree doing — a bare gerund needs a preposition first: agreed on meeting at noon, not ✗ agreed meeting at noon.
entries.a british frame, not an american one: transitive agree with no preposition — We agreed a price, The parties agreed the wording, They agreed a deal — is standard in British and Irish English and in international commercial writing, but it is not ordinary American English. In American prose write agreed on a price or agreed to the wording. The passive the terms were agreed carries the same British flavor; the terms were agreed on is the American form.
entries.to, with, on — the three prepositions: agree to a proposal (you accept it), agree with a person or an opinion (you share it), agree on a matter still being settled (you reach a common position). I agreed to the plan means I went along with it; I agree with the plan means I think it is right; we agreed on a plan means we produced one.
entries.who does the action: with the infinitive, the subject of agree is the one who acts: She agreed to drive — she drives. To report agreement about somebody else, use the that-clause: She agreed that Marcus would drive.
entries.reports: acceptance of a proposal or a statement — the plain, unmarked member of this group, with none of the reluctance of acquiesce, the formality of assent, or the permission-granting of consent.
entries.see also: accept, consent, concur, assent, accede, refuse, promise

examples: We arranged to meet in the lobby half an hour before the talk.
She arranged for the piano to be moved while we were out of town.
The clerk arranged that the deed be recorded the same day.
They still haven't arranged who is covering the front desk.
He arranged the whole trip in a single afternoon.
I've arranged for a neighbor to feed the cat.
entries.русский: договориться, условиться — заранее устроить дело с кем-то ещё
entries.patterns: arrange + to-infinitive · arrange + for + person + to-infinitive · arrange + that-clause (subjunctive) · arrange + wh-clause · arrange + noun phrase
entries.never: arrange someone to do something — arrange cannot take a bare personal object before the infinitive; it needs for. ✗ I arranged him to meet you at the gate → I arranged for him to meet you at the gate, or I arranged that he meet you at the gate.
entries.subjunctive: the that-clause after arrange is mandative, so American English uses the bare base form: arranged that a car be waiting, not that a car was waiting. See the mandative subjunctive.
entries.reports: a commitment that has been settled with somebody else — it reports the outcome of a negotiation, where promise reports a one-sided pledge and agree reports the moment of assent.

examples: The trustees assented to the sale without discussion.
She assented with a single nod and said nothing more.
Both parties assented to having the hearing moved to Thursday.
He would not assent to any version of the text that named him.
The governor assented to the bill on the last day of the session.
Nobody in the room assented, and the motion died.
entries.русский: дать согласие, одобрить — офиц./книжн.: формальное согласие, зафиксированное публично
entries.patterns: assent (intransitive) · assent + to + noun phrase · assent + to + -ing
entries.never: assent to do something and assent that — no infinitive complement and no that-clause, and no direct object. Repairs: assented to the proposal, assented to having the room searched.
entries.homophone: assent and ascent are pronounced identically. The verb of agreement is the one with two s's in the middle; ascent is a climb and is only ever a noun.
entries.mostly a noun: in ordinary American English the noun is far commoner than the verb: she nodded her assent, royal assent, by common assent. The verb belongs to formal narrative and legal prose.
entries.reports: official or public agreement, usually to something formally put — where agree is a position, assent is an act performed on the record.
entries.see also: agree, accede, consent, concur, endorse, second

examples: The mechanic assured us that the noise was nothing serious.
She assured the family of her complete discretion.
I assure you, nobody outside this room has seen the draft.
He assured the board that the audit would be finished before the annual meeting.
They assured her of a full refund and then stopped answering her calls.
Let me assure you that we take every one of these reports seriously.
entries.русский: заверить, уверить — обязательно с лицом: снять чьи-то сомнения (assure smb that)
entries.type: reporting verb — reassurance, guarantee of truth
entries.patterns: assure + person + that-clause · assure + person + of + noun phrase · assure + person (alone, in I assure you)
entries.never: assure that… with no object — assure always names the person reassured. ✗ He assured that the figures were correct → He assured the committee that the figures were correct, or He guaranteed that the figures were correct. Also assure someone to do something: ✗ She assured me to come → She assured me that she would come, or She promised to come.
entries.assure / ensure / insure: assure takes a person and removes their doubt; ensure takes a fact and makes it certain (ensure that the door is locked); insure is about insurance policies. Only assure requires a personal object.
entries.reports: a statement made to remove somebody's doubt — it reports confidence offered rather than a commitment undertaken, which is what separates it from promise.

examples: She chose to finish the degree part-time rather than take a year off.
The witness chose not to answer the last three questions.
They chose the smaller apartment because of the light.
The department chose her to lead the review.
He couldn't choose which of the two offers to take.
You may choose between a refund and a replacement.
entries.русский: выбрать, предпочесть — выбор между реальными вариантами; chose not to = «предпочёл не»
entries.patterns: choose + to-infinitive · choose + not to-infinitive · choose + noun phrase · choose + person + to-infinitive (= select) · choose + wh-clause · choose + between/among + noun phrase
entries.never: choose that and choose doing — no that-clause and no gerund. ✗ He chose that he would stay → He chose to stay. ✗ She chose staying → She chose to stay.
entries.irregular: choose / chose / chosen. The present is /tʃuz/ and the past is /tʃoʊz/ — the vowel is the only thing that separates them in speech, and the spelling choosed does not exist.
entries.reporting a refusal politely: chose not to is the standard neutral way to report a declined action without the flat force of refused: He chose not to comment is journalistically careful; He refused to comment is not.
entries.reports: a decision taken between real alternatives, with the emphasis on the option not taken — decide names the moment of resolution, choose names the selection.

examples: The city committed to replacing every lead service line within ten years.
She committed herself to the project before she saw the budget.
Neither side would commit to a date.
They've committed to a full audit, and the letter says so in writing.
He was committed to finishing the trail before the first snow.
Don't commit to anything until you've read the second page.
entries.русский: обязаться, взять на себя обязательство — обычно публично и от лица организации
entries.register: neutral, common in business and political writing
entries.patterns: commit + to + -ing · commit + to + noun phrase · commit + oneself + to + -ing / noun phrase · commit + person / organization + to + -ing / noun phrase (committed the company to a full audit) · passive: be committed to + -ing
entries.never: commit that… — no that-clause: ✗ They committed that they would hire locally → They committed to hiring locally, or They promised that they would hire locally. And commit someone to do something — when an object is present, to is still the preposition, so what follows is a noun or an -ing: ✗ The deal commits the buyer to pay the fees → The deal commits the buyer to paying the fees. There is no frame in which commit is followed by a bare to-infinitive clause of its own.
entries.commit to do or commit to doing — contes: the textbook rule is that to here is a preposition, so a gerund must follow: committed to reducing emissions. Corporate and political English breaks this constantly — committed to reduce emissions appears in press releases every day, and reads as unremarkable to most Americans. It is still the form editors change, so write the -ing in anything that will be edited.
entries.the other commit: commit a crime, commit funds, commit to memory are unrelated senses with a plain direct object. Doubling: committed, committing, commitment — but commitment keeps a single t before -ment.
entries.reports: a binding undertaking, usually institutional and usually public — promise is what a person says to another person; commit is what an organization puts on the record.

examples: The second reviewer concurred that the methodology was sound.
Two of the three judges concurred in the judgment but wrote separately.
I concur with everything my colleague has just said.
The panel concurred on the diagnosis within an hour.
She read the report twice and concurred.
The auditors did not concur that the reserve was adequate.
entries.русский: согласиться с мнением — книжн./юр.: разделять оценку, но не обещать действие
entries.type: reporting verb — agreement with a statement or judgment
entries.patterns: concur (intransitive) · concur + that-clause · concur + with + person / opinion · concur + in + noun phrase (legal) · concur + on + noun phrase
entries.never: concur to do something — no infinitive, because concur reports shared opinion, never a commitment to act. ✗ The two agencies concurred to release the data → The two agencies agreed to release the data. It also takes no direct object: ✗ I concur your assessment → I concur with your assessment.
entries.spelling: the final consonant doubles: concurred, concurring. The noun is concurrence.
entries.legal sense: in American appellate opinions, a judge who concurs in the judgment agrees with the outcome but not necessarily the reasoning — a technical distinction that the everyday agree cannot make.
entries.reports: agreement with an assessment or a judgment already stated — it never reports agreement to do anything, which is precisely what separates it from agree.

examples: The patient consented to the procedure after reading the risks.
Her parents consented to her taking the internship abroad.
He consented to testify only under subpoena.
No landowner along the route has consented.
She consented to the sale of the property but not to the terms of the lease.
Both parties consented to having the dispute heard by an arbitrator.
entries.русский: дать согласие, разрешить — согласие на то, что сделают с тобой; юр. и мед. термин
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard verb in legal and medical contexts
entries.type: reporting verb — permission, agreement to something affecting oneself
entries.patterns: consent + to-infinitive · consent + to + noun phrase · consent + to + -ing · consent (intransitive)
entries.never: consent someone to do something — no personal object. ✗ The judge consented her to travel → The judge allowed her to travel or The judge consented to her traveling. Consent that… survives only in old legal formulas (consents that judgment be entered); in ordinary modern English write agreed that.
entries.two kinds of to: consent takes both an infinitive to and a prepositional to, with almost the same meaning: consented to be interviewed and consented to being interviewed are both standard. Very few verbs allow this pair — compare refuse, which allows only the infinitive.
entries.stress: the verb is kuhn-SENT; there is no noun/verb stress shift, unlike reject and refuse.
entries.reports: permission granted for something that will be done to you or in your name — where agree accepts a proposal, consent authorizes an act.

examples: We decided to leave before the traffic started.
He decided that the whole thing had been a misunderstanding.
They still haven't decided where to hold the ceremony.
She decided against saying anything until she had the paperwork.
The panel decided the appeal in under a week.
I decided not to renew the lease.
entries.русский: решить, принять решение — нейтральное слово; также «разрешить дело» (о суде)
entries.patterns: decide + to-infinitive · decide + not to-infinitive · decide + that-clause · decide + wh-clause · decide + on/against + noun phrase / -ing · decide + noun phrase (a case, a question)
entries.never: decide someone to do something — no personal object before the infinitive. ✗ The letter decided me to go → The letter decided me (object alone, fine) or The letter made me decide to go. Also decide doing: a gerund needs a preposition — decided on selling the house, not ✗ decided selling the house.
entries.the negative: decided not to is a decision against acting; didn't decide to is the absence of a decision. She decided not to call and She didn't decide to call are not paraphrases of each other.
entries.two senses: decide also means settle a question and takes a plain object: the court decided the case, one goal decided the match. In that sense the subject is often not a speaker at all.
entries.reports: the moment a course of action is fixed — where choose highlights the alternatives and resolve the determination, decide is the neutral, ordinary word.
entries.see also: resolve, determine, choose, opt, elect, arrange

examples: The senator declined to say whether she had spoken to the mayor.
He declined the invitation but sent flowers.
Both witnesses declined to be photographed.
She was offered the chairmanship twice and declined both times.
The company declined to confirm the number of layoffs.
I declined, as politely as I knew how.
entries.русский: вежливо отказаться, отклонить — учтивый отказ без вызова; станд. в журналистике
entries.patterns: decline + to-infinitive · decline + noun phrase · decline (intransitive)
entries.never: decline doing and decline that — no gerund and no that-clause. ✗ He declined commenting → He declined to comment. ✗ She declined that she would attend → She declined the invitation or She said she would not attend. It also cannot take two objects: ✗ They declined him the loan → They refused him the loan or They denied him the loan. And no personal object before the infinitive — decline someone to do something: ✗ She declined me to speak → She declined to let me speak.
entries.the newsroom verb: declined to comment is the fixed formula because refused to comment implies the reporter was entitled to an answer. The choice between the two verbs is an editorial judgment, not a stylistic one.
entries.the other decline: decline also means fall (sales declined, a declining population), which is intransitive and unrelated to speech.
entries.reports: refusal offered courteously, with no suggestion of defiance — refuse reports a blocked demand, decline reports an offer not taken up.
entries.see also: refuse, reject, turn down, demur, accept, spurn

examples: When I suggested splitting the cost, he demurred.
She demurred at the suggestion that the delay was her doing.
The committee demurred to the chair's reading of the bylaws.
"That seems a little steep," she demurred.
He demurred at paying in advance and asked for an invoice instead.
Nobody demurred, so the motion carried.
entries.русский: замяться, мягко возразить — книжн.: нерешительное возражение, ещё не отказ
entries.patterns: demur (intransitive) · demur + at + noun phrase / -ing · demur + to + noun phrase · direct speech attribution: "…," he demurred.
entries.never: demur to do something and demur that — no infinitive and no that-clause; the objection is never spelled out by a complement clause. ✗ She demurred that it was too expensive → She demurred at the price or She objected that it was too expensive.
entries.spelling and stress: stress on the second syllable throughout, and the r doubles: demurred, demurring, demurral. Not to be confused with the adjective demure /dɪˈmjʊr/, which means modest and is a different word entirely.
entries.as a speech tag: demurred is one of the few verbs in this group used to attribute direct speech: "I'm not sure that's fair," she demurred. It signals a soft, hedged objection.
entries.reports: a mild, hesitant objection rather than a refusal — the speaker balks but has not yet said no, which is exactly what refuse and decline have already done.

examples: He determined to learn the language before the posting began.
The inspector determined that the wiring had never been permitted.
We could not determine who had signed the form.
The court will determine the amount of damages next month.
She had determined on a complete change of career.
They were determined to have the roof finished before the rain.
entries.русский: твёрдо решить — книжн.; чаще: установить, заключить (determine that — о факте)
entries.type: reporting verb — firm decision; also a finding
entries.patterns: determine + to-infinitive · determine + that-clause · determine + wh-clause · determine + noun phrase · determine + on/upon + noun phrase · passive: be determined to + infinitive
entries.never: determine someone to do something — no personal object before the infinitive. ✗ The evidence determined the jury to acquit → The evidence led the jury to acquit. Also determine doing: determined on selling, not ✗ determined selling.
entries.two speech acts in one verb: determine reports a decision (He determined to see it through) and, far more often in modern American English, a finding (The lab determined that the sample was contaminated). Only the first belongs in this group; the second is a verb of establishing fact, and the that-clause is what tells you which is meant.
entries.the passive is commoner than the active: in the resolve sense, be determined to has almost replaced the plain active verb: She was determined to finish is ordinary English; She determined to finish reads as literary or nineteenth-century.
entries.reports: a decision arrived at and held to — stronger than decide, and unlike resolve it doubles as the verb for reaching a factual conclusion.

examples: Employees who elect to enroll must do so before the fifteenth.
He elected not to appeal the ruling.
She elected to have the surgery in January rather than wait.
Most of the partners elected to defer their distributions.
The taxpayer may elect to spread the gain over four years.
Two of the three defendants elected to testify.
entries.русский: предпочесть, сделать выбор — офиц.: выбрать один из вариантов (не «избирать» кого-то)
entries.register: formal, common in legal, financial, and medical writing
entries.patterns: elect + to-infinitive · elect + not to-infinitive · elect + person (+ as / to) + noun phrase (= vote in)
entries.never: elect that and elect doing — no that-clause and no gerund. ✗ They elected that the case be reheard → They decided that the case be reheard. ✗ He elected taking the buyout → He elected to take the buyout. Nor elect for on the model of opt for: ✗ She elected for the lump sum → She opted for the lump sum or She elected to take the lump sum. Of the three choice verbs, only opt has the for frame.
entries.not the same as voting: the two senses share a spelling and nothing else. The board elected to defer the dividend is a decision by the board; The board elected a new chair is a vote. Only the first is a reporting verb.
entries.reports: a formal choice between options that were both genuinely available — the register of pension paperwork and surgical consent forms, where choose would be too plain.

examples: Three former governors endorsed the ballot measure.
The academy has never endorsed a commercial product.
She endorsed the report's conclusions but not its tone.
He refused to endorse anyone in the primary.
The paper endorsed the bond issue in an editorial on Sunday.
Two of the co-authors declined to endorse the final draft.
entries.русский: публично поддержать, одобрить — открыто заявить о поддержке своим именем
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in politics and journalism
entries.patterns: endorse + noun phrase · endorse + noun phrase + for + office · passive: be endorsed by + person
entries.never: endorse that and endorse to do something — endorse takes only a noun phrase. ✗ The union endorsed that the strike continue → The union endorsed the strike or The union agreed that the strike should continue. To endorse a statement, name it: endorsed the claim that…, endorsed her account of the meeting.
entries.spelling: endorse is the standard American spelling in every sense; indorse survives only in some legal and banking documents. The noun is endorsement.
entries.the check sense: endorse a check — sign the back — is the literal original and takes the same plain object.
entries.reports: public, attributable agreement that lends the speaker's own standing to something — agree is a private position, endorse is a position taken on somebody else's behalf.

examples: The shop guarantees that every repair is good for ninety days.
She guaranteed us a full refund if the tour was canceled.
The printer guaranteed to have the programs ready by Thursday morning.
No coach can guarantee a starting position.
He guaranteed the loan personally, which is why the bank agreed to it.
I can't guarantee that anyone will be in the office on Friday.
entries.русский: гарантировать — обещать с гарантией: обещание, подкреплённое ответственностью
entries.type: reporting verb — promise with a warranty behind it
entries.patterns: guarantee + that-clause · guarantee + person + that-clause · guarantee + to-infinitive · guarantee + noun phrase · guarantee + person + noun phrase
entries.never: guarantee someone to do something — the personal object can precede a that-clause or a noun, never an infinitive. ✗ They guaranteed us to deliver by Friday → They guaranteed us that they would deliver by Friday, or They guaranteed to deliver by Friday, or They guaranteed us delivery by Friday.
entries.stress and spelling: the stress is on the last syllable, gair-uhn-TEE, and the word ends -ee, not -ie. The variant guaranty is not a British spelling — it is an older form now confined to American banking, finance, and legal drafting (a guaranty of payment) and to fixed corporate names such as Guaranty Trust. It is a noun there, not the verb; for the reporting verb, write guarantee in both British and American English.
entries.not always a speech act: guarantee often reports a state of affairs rather than an utterance: Rain doesn't guarantee a cancellation. Only the human-subject uses are reporting verbs.
entries.reports: a promise backed by something the speaker will forfeit if it fails — where promise stakes credibility, guarantee stakes money or a remedy.

examples: The doctor insisted that he stay off the ankle for two weeks.
She insisted that the check had been mailed on the first.
He insisted on paying for dinner and would not hear another word about it.
They insisted on seeing the original document, not a copy.
I offered to walk, but she insisted.
The airline insists that every passenger be at the gate forty minutes early.
entries.русский: настаивать — требовать (с сослагательным); либо упорно утверждать вопреки сомнениям
entries.type: reporting verb — demand, or firm assertion
entries.patterns: insist + that-clause (subjunctive = demand) · insist + that-clause (indicative = assertion) · insist + on/upon + noun phrase · insist + on/upon + -ing · insist (intransitive)
entries.never: insist to do something and insist someone to do something — insist takes no infinitive at all, and no personal object. ✗ He insisted me to stay → He insisted that I stay or He insisted on my staying. ✗ She insisted to pay → She insisted on paying. It takes no direct object either: ✗ I insist my innocence → I insist on my innocence.
entries.two verbs in one, and the clause tells y: with a bare subjunctive the verb demands: He insisted that she be there by nine. With an indicative it asserts, against doubt: He insisted that she was there by nine. Same verb, same that, opposite speech acts — and the second one backshifts normally while the first cannot backshift at all. See the mandative subjunctive and insist in the no-backshift rules.
entries.the demand sense in the negative: the negative goes in front of the bare verb, with no do: She insisted that we not tell the press — never ✗ that we don't tell or ✗ that we didn't tell.
entries.reports: either an unyielding demand or a claim pressed against resistance — in both senses it presupposes that somebody has pushed back, which plain say and ask do not.

examples: She offered to look after the dog while we were away.
They offered him the job on the spot.
He offered no explanation for the missing hours.
The airline offered a voucher, which nobody wanted.
I offered to pay half and he wouldn't take it.
Somebody in the back row finally offered.
entries.русский: предложить, вызваться — самому предложить услугу или вещь, пока не попросили
entries.patterns: offer + to-infinitive · offer + noun phrase · offer + person + noun phrase · offer + noun phrase + to + person · offer (intransitive)
entries.never: offer someone to do something — with the infinitive, offer allows no object at all, because the person who will act is always the subject. ✗ He offered me to drive → He offered to drive, or, naming the beneficiary with a noun, He offered me a ride. Also offer doing: ✗ She offered helping → She offered to help.
entries.that-clause: offer + that is rare and stilted in American English. ✗ He offered that we could stay is better as He said we could stay or He invited us to stay.
entries.who acts: offer to always means the subject will do it: She offered to call him — she calls. Compare promise, which works the same way, and tell, which does not.
entries.reports: a service or a thing volunteered before it was asked for — where promise commits to something already expected, offer initiates.
entries.see also: volunteer, promise, agree, accept, decline, turn down

examples: Most families opted for the later session.
He opted to walk rather than wait forty minutes for a bus.
You can opt out of the mailing list at any time.
The school opted to close for the day.
She opted in to the pilot program on the first morning.
Faced with two bad choices, they opted for the cheaper one.
entries.русский: выбрать, предпочесть — разг./газетное; opt to + инфинитив, opt for + существительное
entries.patterns: opt + to-infinitive · opt + for + noun phrase · opt + out (of) + noun phrase · opt + in (to) + noun phrase
entries.never: opt that, opt doing, and a bare object — opt never takes a clause, a gerund, or a direct object. ✗ She opted taking the earlier flight → She opted to take the earlier flight or She opted for the earlier flight. ✗ They opted the smaller model → They opted for the smaller model. And opt someone to do something — no personal object: ✗ The chair opted her to present → The chair chose her to present.
entries.for + noun, to + verb: the two frames divide cleanly: a noun after for, a verb after to. He opted for surgery and He opted to have surgery say the same thing with different grammar.
entries.reports: a choice made when a real alternative was on the table — briefer and more newspaper-like than choose, and without the formality of elect.

examples: The foundation pledged two million dollars over four years.
She pledged to serve only one term.
The company pledged that no jobs would be moved overseas.
Donors pledged more than the campaign had asked for.
He pledged himself to silence about what he had seen.
Both candidates pledged to release their tax returns.
entries.русский: публично обещать, обязаться — офиц./газетное, часто о деньгах и политике
entries.register: pledge is a headline word. In speech people promise; in print, governments, donors, and candidates pledge. Using it of a private conversation sounds ceremonial: He pledged to take out the trash is a joke.
entries.patterns: pledge + to-infinitive · pledge + that-clause · pledge + noun phrase · pledge + person + noun phrase · pledge + person or oneself + to + noun phrase / -ing (pledged himself to secrecy, pledged them to silence)
entries.never: pledge someone to do something — the personal object is a recipient of what is pledged, not the subject of an infinitive. ✗ They pledged us to rebuild the school → They pledged to rebuild the school or They pledged us the money for the school. What looks like an exception is not one: in He pledged himself to secrecy and She pledged them to silence, the to is a preposition taking a noun, so an -ing may follow it (pledged them to saying nothing) but a bare infinitive never can.
entries.reports: a promise made publicly, often with an obligation attached — promise is between people, pledge is on the record and usually about money or policy.
entries.see also: promise, vow, swear, commit, undertake, guarantee

examples: He promised to call as soon as the plane landed.
She promised me that nobody else would see the file.
The contractor promised a finished kitchen by Thanksgiving.
I promise I won't say a word.
They promised the neighbors a full report and never delivered one.
Don't promise anything you can't put in writing.
entries.русский: обещать — обычное обещание: говорящий ручается своей надёжностью
entries.patterns: promise + to-infinitive · promise + that-clause · promise + person + that-clause · promise + person + noun phrase · promise + noun phrase · promise (intransitive: I promise)
entries.never: promise doing — no gerund: ✗ He promised calling → He promised to call. And promise someone to do something, while attested and grammatical in older English, is effectively dead: ?He promised me to be there is avoided. American English names the addressee with a that-clause instead — He promised me that he would be there — or drops the addressee — He promised to be there.
entries.it absorbs will: promise already contains the future, so the would of ordinary backshift disappears into the infinitive: He said he would pay me back and He promised to pay me back report the same sentence. See Backshift.
entries.no backshift on a live promise: if the commitment is still outstanding, the present often survives: She promised she is coming is ordinary speech when she has not yet arrived. See When not to backshift.
entries.that-drop: that is dropped freely after promise in speech: I promise I'll be there.
entries.reports: a commitment by the speaker to do something, staking their reliability on it — where offer proposes and agree accepts, promise binds.
entries.see also: pledge, vow, swear, guarantee, assure, undertake, commit, threaten

examples: He refused to give his name to the officer.
The bank refused her application without explaining why.
She refused the promotion twice before finally taking it.
They refused us entry because the doors had already closed.
The engine refused to start in the cold.
I asked three times and he refused every time.
entries.русский: отказаться, отказать — резкое «нет» на требование; из клауз только refuse to + инф.
entries.patterns: refuse + to-infinitive · refuse + noun phrase · refuse + person + noun phrase · refuse (intransitive)
entries.never: refuse that, refuse doing, and refuse someone to do something — this is the tightest verb in the group. Among clause complements, refuse takes the to-infinitive and nothing else. ✗ She refused that she would sign → She refused to sign. ✗ He refused paying → He refused to pay. ✗ They refused him to enter → They refused him entry or They would not let him enter.
entries.the two objects that are allowed: refuse takes a noun object (refused the offer) and even two (refused him a visa) — what it will not take is a clause. Learners who know refused to sign often invent ✗ refused that he sign by analogy with insisted that he sign; there is no such frame.
entries.stress: the verb is rih-FYOOZ, ending in a /z/. The unrelated noun refuse meaning garbage is REF-yooss, /ˈrɛfjus/, stressed on the first syllable.
entries.judgment — it is not a neutral report: refuse presupposes that the speaker was under some obligation to comply, and so reports them as obstructive. He refused to comment tells the reader he owed an answer; He declined to comment tells the reader he did not; He chose not to comment tells the reader nothing about who was owed what. All three can report the same silence, and picking one is an editorial judgment. See decline and choose.
entries.reports: a flat, deliberate no to something demanded, requested, or expected — stronger and less courteous than decline, and unlike reject it refuses an action, not a thing.
entries.see also: decline, reject, turn down, spurn, veto, agree, consent

examples: The journal rejected the paper without sending it out for review.
Voters rejected the measure by a margin of two to one.
He rejected the offer as insulting.
The court rejected the argument that the search had been consensual.
Her insurer rejected the claim on a technicality.
Every proposal we sent was rejected within a week.
entries.русский: отвергнуть, отклонить — отказать предмету (предложению, заявке) с оценкой «негодно»
entries.type: reporting verb — rejection of a proposal, claim, or application
entries.patterns: reject + noun phrase · reject + noun phrase + as + adjective / noun · reject + the claim / idea / suggestion + that-clause (the that-clause belongs to the noun, not the verb) · passive: be rejected
entries.never: reject to do something and reject doing — no infinitive and no gerund: ✗ He rejected to comment → He declined to comment. And reject takes a that-clause only through a noun: ✗ She rejected that the data was flawed → She rejected the claim that the data was flawed, or She denied that the data was flawed.
entries.stress shift: the verb is rih-JEKT; the noun is REE-jekt /ˈridʒɛkt/. This is the regular two-syllable noun/verb stress pattern of record, permit, conflict.
entries.thing, not action: reject refuses a thing put forward — an offer, a bid, a manuscript, an argument. To refuse an action, use refuse to or decline to.
entries.reports: a considered refusal of something formally put forward, often with a judgment that it was not good enough — decline is polite, turn down is neutral, reject is a verdict.
entries.see also: refuse, decline, turn down, veto, spurn, accept

examples: She resolved to say nothing until the lawyer arrived.
The assembly resolved that no further funds be released.
After the second breakdown, we resolved on selling the car.
He resolved to be at the gym by six every morning, and lasted nine days.
They resolved the dispute without going to court.
The committee could not resolve how to allocate the remaining seats.
entries.русский: твёрдо решить — решимость не отступать; также «постановить» (о собрании, книжн.)
entries.type: reporting verb — firm decision; formal motion
entries.patterns: resolve + to-infinitive · resolve + that-clause (subjunctive, in motions) · resolve + on/upon + noun phrase / -ing · resolve + noun phrase (= settle) · resolve + wh-clause
entries.never: resolve someone to do something — no personal object before the infinitive: ✗ The speech resolved them to act → The speech made them resolve to act. Also resolve doing: resolved on moving, not ✗ resolved moving.
entries.subjunctive in motions: the that-clause of a formal resolution is mandative and takes the bare form: The board resolved that the position be eliminated — the Resolved, that… of parliamentary minutes. See the mandative subjunctive.
entries.the other resolve: resolve a dispute, resolve an image, resolve into — all unrelated to speech, and all with a plain object.
entries.reports: a decision made with an act of will behind it — decide records the choice, resolve records the determination not to go back on it.

examples: Ramirez moved to adjourn and Chen seconded.
The nomination was seconded before the chair had finished speaking.
"I'll second that," he said, reaching for his coffee.
No one seconded the motion, so it was not debated.
She seconded the proposal but voted against it an hour later.
Every motion has to be seconded to reach the floor.
entries.русский: поддержать предложение — парлам.: официально присоединиться к чужому предложению
entries.register: formal, parliamentary; also informal in I'll second that
entries.type: reporting verb — formal agreement with a proposal
entries.patterns: second + noun phrase (a motion, a nomination, a proposal) · second + that (as a pronoun: I second that)
entries.never: second that we adjourn as a clause — the that in I second that is a demonstrative pronoun, not a complementizer, so nothing can follow it. ✗ He seconded that the meeting be adjourned → He seconded the motion to adjourn. Also no infinitive and no gerund: ✗ She seconded to postpone → She seconded the proposal to postpone.
entries.a different verb with the same spelling: British English has second /sɪˈkɑnd/, stressed on the second syllable, meaning to transfer an employee temporarily (seconded to the Treasury). It is rare in American use and is a separate word from the parliamentary verb.
entries.why it exists: under standard parliamentary procedure a motion cannot be debated until someone else supports it. Second reports that specific, procedurally necessary act of agreement — no other verb in this group does.
entries.reports: formal support for somebody else's motion, given so that it can proceed — narrower than endorse, and unlike agree it is an act with a procedural consequence.

examples: He spurned every attempt his family made to reach him.
The novelist spurned the prize and said so in a letter to the committee.
She spurned his apology and walked out.
Voters spurned the incumbent for the first time in thirty years.
The club spurned an offer twice what the player was worth.
Having been spurned once, he did not ask again.
entries.русский: отвергнуть с презрением — книжн.: отказ, окрашенный пренебрежением к предложенному
entries.patterns: spurn + noun phrase · passive: be spurned
entries.never: spurn to do something, spurn doing, and spurn that — spurn takes a noun phrase and nothing else. ✗ He spurned to answer → He refused to answer. ✗ She spurned that the offer was generous → She rejected the suggestion that the offer was generous.
entries.register warning: spurn carries scorn on the part of the refuser and is at home in fiction, opinion writing, and headlines. In a neutral report it editorializes: She spurned the offer tells the reader how to feel about her; She declined the offer does not.
entries.reports: rejection delivered with contempt — the only verb in the group whose meaning includes the refuser's disdain for what was offered.
entries.see also: reject, refuse, decline, turn down, veto

examples: The witness swore that she had never met the defendant.
He swore to tell the whole story once the case was closed.
She swore us all to secrecy before opening the envelope.
I swear I put the keys on the hook.
Every officer swears an oath before taking the badge.
He swore he would never set foot in that building again.
entries.русский: поклясться; божиться — торжественно обещать либо клятвенно утверждать
entries.register: neutral to formal; both an everyday intensifier and a courtroom term
entries.type: reporting verb — solemn promise or solemn assertion
entries.patterns: swear + to-infinitive · swear + that-clause · swear + noun phrase (an oath, allegiance, revenge) · swear + to + noun phrase · swear + person + to + noun phrase (swore us to secrecy) · swear + on + noun phrase (on the Bible) · swear (intransitive) · swear + at + person (= curse) · swear + by + noun phrase (= trust utterly)
entries.never: swear someone to do something — the personal object takes to + a noun, never an infinitive. ✗ He swore me to keep quiet → He swore me to silence, or He made me promise to keep quiet. Also swear doing: ✗ She swore telling no one → She swore to tell no one.
entries.irregular: swear / swore / sworn. The past participle appears in the fixed legal phrases a sworn statement, sworn testimony, duly sworn.
entries.three unrelated senses: promise solemnly (swore to repay it), assert emphatically (I swear I locked it), and use obscene language (swore at the referee). Only the first two are reporting verbs, and the preposition tells them apart from the third.
entries.everyday use: in speech I swear is mostly an intensifier attached to an ordinary claim — I swear I sent it — and reports insistence rather than an oath.
entries.reports: a promise or an assertion made under an oath, real or rhetorical — it reports the speaker invoking a penalty for being wrong, which promise and say do not.
entries.see also: vow, pledge, promise, guarantee, assure, insist

examples: He threatened to resign if the report was published.
She threatened the contractor with a lawsuit and he finished the job that week.
The union threatened a strike for the first day of the season.
They threatened that the case would go to collections.
The sky threatened rain all afternoon and never delivered.
Nobody threatened anyone; it was a disagreement about a parking space.
entries.русский: угрожать, пригрозить — зеркало promise: обещание того, что слушателю нежелательно
entries.patterns: threaten + to-infinitive · threaten + that-clause · threaten + person · threaten + person + with + noun phrase · threaten + noun phrase (an action, a consequence) · inanimate subject: it threatened to rain
entries.never: threaten someone to do something — the personal object and the infinitive cannot appear together, because the infinitive names what the threatener will do, not what the victim must do. ✗ He threatened her to leave has no possible reading. Repairs, depending on the meaning: He threatened to leave (he will go), He threatened her with dismissal (he named her penalty), He told her to leave (he ordered her out).
entries.the mirror image of promise: threaten and promise have the same grammar and opposite content: both commit the subject to a future act, one welcome and one not. He promised to call the police and He threatened to call the police differ only in whose interest the call serves.
entries.conditionals collapse into it: a threat is usually an if-sentence, and the verb absorbs the whole structure: "If you print that, I'll sue" → He threatened to sue if we printed it. See reporting conditionals.
entries.not always speech: with a non-human subject threaten reports an omen rather than an utterance: The clouds threatened rain, The strike threatened to shut down the port.
entries.reports: a commitment to do something the listener does not want, made in order to change their behavior — the negative counterpart of promise, and unlike warn it names the speaker as the source of the harm.
entries.see also: warn, promise, swear, vow, insist, refuse

examples: She turned down a full scholarship to stay near her mother.
They offered him twice the salary and he turned it down.
The zoning board turned down the application for the third time.
I'd turn down anything that meant moving in January.
He was turned down by four banks before one said yes.
You don't turn down an invitation like that without a reason.
entries.русский: отклонить, отказаться от — разг.: обычный отказ от предложенного (работы, приглашения)
entries.type: reporting verb — refusal of an offer or request (phrasal verb, separable)
entries.patterns: turn down + noun phrase · turn + noun phrase + down · turn + pronoun + down (obligatory order) · passive: be turned down
entries.never: turn down it — with a pronoun object the two halves must split: turned it down, never ✗ turned down it. With a full noun phrase either order works: turned down the job / turned the job down. And like the other noun-only refusal verbs, turn down to do something and turn down that are impossible: ✗ He turned down to comment → He declined to comment.
entries.long objects go last: although both orders are allowed with a noun, a long object almost always goes after the particle: She turned down the offer that the university had spent a month putting together — the split version strands down too far from its verb.
entries.other senses: turn down the heat, turn down a collar, turn down a bed are literal and unrelated. Only the refusal sense reports speech.
entries.reports: refusal of something offered, in ordinary conversational register — the everyday equivalent of reject, without its verdict-like weight or the politeness of decline.
entries.see also: reject, decline, refuse, spurn, accept, offer

examples: The tenant undertakes to return the property in the condition received.
She undertook to deliver the manuscript by the end of the year.
The company undertook that no personal data would leave the country.
He undertook the negotiation himself rather than send a deputy.
Neither party has undertaken to cover the other's costs.
They undertook a complete review of the safety procedures.
entries.русский: обязаться, принять на себя — офиц./юр.: обещание, закреплённое в договоре
entries.patterns: undertake + to-infinitive · undertake + that-clause · undertake + noun phrase (= take on a task)
entries.never: undertake someone to do something — no personal object: ✗ The seller undertakes the buyer to insure the goods → The seller undertakes to insure the goods, or The seller undertakes that the goods will be insured. In the promise sense there is also no gerund: ✗ He undertook paying the costs → He undertook to pay the costs.
entries.two senses, two frames: with an infinitive or a that-clause it is a promise (undertook to repay the loan); with a plain noun object it means take on a piece of work (undertook a survey of the site). Only the first is a reporting verb.
entries.reports: a promise given in a formal or contractual setting, where breaking it has consequences that are written down — the register of promise in a document rather than a conversation.
entries.see also: promise, pledge, guarantee, commit, agree, arrange

examples: The president vetoed the spending bill on the last day of the session.
Two members of the council vetoed the whole redevelopment plan.
She vetoed the idea of a surprise party before anyone could argue.
The measure was vetoed and never came back to the floor.
Any permanent member may veto a resolution.
He vetoed three of the four names on the shortlist.
entries.русский: наложить вето, заблокировать — отказ того, чья власть окончательно закрывает вопрос
entries.register: neutral to formal; political and institutional
entries.patterns: veto + noun phrase · passive: be vetoed
entries.never: veto that, veto to do something, and veto doing — veto takes a noun phrase naming what is blocked, and nothing else. ✗ She vetoed that we go to the lake → She vetoed the trip to the lake. ✗ He vetoed spending more → He vetoed the extra spending. It also does not take a person: ✗ The governor vetoed the legislature → The governor vetoed the bill.
entries.spelling: vetoes, vetoed, vetoing — the third person takes -es, like echoes and goes.
entries.informal use: outside government, veto is used lightly for anyone with the power to block a plan: My wife vetoed the orange couch. The joke is the mismatch of register.
entries.reports: rejection by someone with the standing to block a thing outright — reject is a judgment, veto is an exercise of power, and it ends the matter.
entries.see also: reject, refuse, turn down, decline, second, endorse

examples: Two students volunteered to help set up the chairs.
He volunteered that he had never actually read the contract.
My brother volunteered me to drive everyone to the airport.
She volunteered the name of the supplier before anyone asked for it.
Nobody volunteered, so the chair assigned the task.
They volunteered for the night shift because it paid more.
entries.русский: вызваться; сообщить без просьбы — предложить помощь или выдать сведения по своей воле
entries.type: reporting verb — unprompted offer, unprompted statement
entries.patterns: volunteer + to-infinitive · volunteer + person + to-infinitive · volunteer + that-clause · volunteer + noun phrase (information, help, a name) · volunteer + for + noun phrase · volunteer (intransitive)
entries.never: volunteer doing — no gerund: ✗ He volunteered driving us to the airport → He volunteered to drive us to the airport. Note what is allowed and often surprises learners: volunteer does take a personal object before the infinitive — My manager volunteered me to run the meeting — which offer, its nearest neighbor, flatly refuses.
entries.two speech acts: volunteer covers offering to act (volunteered to stay late) and offering information nobody asked for (volunteered that he had been there that night). The second is the sense that matters in reported speech: it marks the statement as unprompted, which is why it appears constantly in accounts of interviews and testimony.
entries.stress: the noun and the verb are stressed identically, on the last syllable: vah-luhn-TEER.
entries.reports: an offer or a disclosure made without being asked — the unprompted is the whole meaning, and no other verb in this group carries it.

examples: The mayor vowed to appeal the ruling within the week.
She vowed that she would never lend him money again.
He vowed revenge on everyone who had testified.
They vowed to rebuild on the same lot.
After the second flood, she vowed to sell the house.
The candidate vowed to serve out the full term.
entries.русский: поклясться, дать зарок — книжн./газетное: торжественное обещание с вызовом или решимостью
entries.patterns: vow + to-infinitive · vow + that-clause · vow + noun phrase (vowed revenge) · vow (intransitive, rare)
entries.never: vow someone to do something and vow doing — no personal object and no gerund. ✗ She vowed him to return → She vowed to return. ✗ He vowed fighting the ruling → He vowed to fight the ruling.
entries.headline verb: vow is short, so newspapers use it where speech would use promise or say: Mayor vows to fight ruling. In running prose it sounds heightened — a person who vows to pick up the dry cleaning is being funny.
entries.the emotional charge: vow usually reports defiance or devotion. He vowed to appeal implies determination against opposition; He promised to appeal implies only an obligation.
entries.reports: a promise made solemnly and usually in public, with feeling behind it — pledge is institutional, swear invokes an oath, and vow carries the speaker's resolve.
entries.see also: swear, pledge, promise, resolve, threaten, determine

examples: The landlord warned them that the next late payment would start eviction.
She warned me not to sign anything before the lawyer had read it.
Regulators warned that the bank was undercapitalized.
He warned us about the ice on the bottom step.
Her attorney warned her against speaking to reporters.
I warned him twice, and after that I stopped.
entries.русский: предупредить, предостеречь — известить о плохом последствии; часто скрытая угроза
entries.type: reporting verb — warning; a threat presented as a prediction
entries.patterns: warn + person + that-clause · warn + that-clause (no object) · warn + person + to-infinitive · warn + person + not to-infinitive · warn + person + of/about + noun phrase · warn + person + against + noun phrase / -ing · warn + person (alone)
entries.never: warn to do something with no object — the infinitive frame requires the person: ✗ He warned to be careful → He warned us to be careful. The that-clause is different: there the object may be dropped, and routinely is in news writing — Forecasters warned that the storm would stall. Also warn someone something: ✗ She warned me the deadline → She warned me about the deadline; and warn someone for doing: ✗ He warned me for being late → He warned me against being late.
entries.the object rule, compared with tell: tell can never drop its personal object; warn can, but only before a that-clause. ✗ He told that the road was closed is wrong, while He warned that the road was closed is perfectly standard.
entries.warning or threat: warn reports a threat when the speaker controls the harm — He warned me that he would go to the police — and an ordinary caution when they do not — He warned me that the steps were icy. Only the first belongs to this group; for the caution and advice sense see Reported commands, requests, and advice.
entries.negative infinitive: not goes before to: warned us not to touch it, never ✗ warned us to not touch it in careful writing.
entries.reports: notice of a bad consequence — the same content as threaten when the speaker will cause the harm, but framed as information rather than as a demand, which is what makes it the more menacing of the two in print.
